bib.title: LADDER: Self-Improving LLMs Through Recursive Problem Decomposition

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "LADDER: Self-Improving LLMs Through Recursive Problem Decomposition", Toby Simonds and Akira Yoshiyama (Tufa Labs). Preprint (arXiv 2503.00735 v3, cs.LG). First author, March 2025 (the PDF is dated March 6, 2025).

COVERAGE: All 13 pages and 47,189 chars were read, including the references and the appendix. The appendix only lists two unsolved exam questions. Figure data points are not in the text, so only the numbers printed in the text or on the axes are usable.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- LADDER (RL on a model-generated tree of easier variants) lifts Llama 3.2 3B from 1% to 82% on held-out integrals.
  number: 82% vs 1% (pass@1) and 2% (pass@10)
  setup: 110 integration problems (about half textbook, half GPT-4o-made), chosen so GPT-4o could solve them and the base model could not. 10 were used for training and 100 for testing, with about 500 variants per training problem. Training used GRPO.
  quote: "LADDER achieved 82% accuracy on the test set, significantly outperforming both the base model with pass@1 sampling (1%) and with pass@10 sampling (2%)."
  where: p.8, §4.1
- RL on the 10 raw problems without variants fails, so the difficulty gradient is the cause and not the RL algorithm.
  number: never above 3%, then 0% within 30 steps
  setup: Llama 3.2 3B, identical hyperparameters to the LADDER run.
  quote: "RL without variants consistently failed, with performance never exceeding 3% before collapsing to 0% within 30 training steps"
  where: p.8
- A 7B model reaches 73% on the 2025 MIT Integration Bee qualifier, up from 50%.
  number: 73% vs a 50% base. GPT-4o scored 42% and o1 scored 80%.
  setup: DeepSeek-R1-distilled Qwen2.5 7B. About 9,000 variants were generated from the 2010-2024 qualifying exams at tree depth 2, with a 70% easier / 30% equivalent mix. The exam has 20 questions. Figure 5 is an average of 3 runs.
  quote: "LADDER improved the accuracy of the Deepseek-R1 Qwen 2.5 7B base model from a baseline of 50% to 73% on the 2025 qualifying examination, significantly outperforming other existing models, including GPT-4o (42%)."
  where: p.9, §4.2
- TTRL (per-question RL on freshly generated variants at test time, then roll back) lifts the 7B model from 73% to 90%.
  number: 90%, from 100 RL steps and about 800 variants per unsolved question
  setup: Applied only to questions LADDER got wrong. A question counts as solved if the model answers it correctly at any point in the 100 steps, as judged by the numerical checker. Two questions stayed unsolved.
  quote: "Of the remaining incorrect responses, TTRL successfully solved 3-4 additional problems, increasing performance from 73% to 90% (Figure 6)."
  where: p.9, §4.3 and §3.2.3
- TTRL beats naive resampling and needs LADDER first.
  number: LADDER pass@100 is below 90% (Figure 6 axis); the exact value is not in the text.
  setup: TTRL applied directly to the pre-LADDER base model for 100 steps.
  quote: "After 100 steps, the base model remained unable to correctly answer any of the questions that LADDER + TTRL successfully solved."
  where: p.10
- Steps needed per unsolved question varied from 3 to 30.
  quote: "ranging from as few as 3 steps to as many as 30"
  where: p.10
- Accuracy keeps rising with the number of variants, with slowing gains past about 6,000.
  setup: Llama 3B, Figure 3 x-axis runs to 9k variants.
  quote: "While the rate of improvement appears to slow beyond 6,000 variants, the data suggests that continued scaling may still yield further gains."
  where: p.8
- Variant generation needs diversity tricks: batches of 10 per prompt, temperature cycling between 0.8 and 1.4, rotating mathematician personas, 3-5 sampled transformations per prompt, and recursion. Plain "make it easier" prompts gave repetitive output.
  quote: "Temperature cycling: We dynamically varied the sampling temperature between 0.8 and 1.4 across prompts."
  where: p.4
- Variant quality control is weak. About 8% of Llama variants were unsolvable within 5 seconds, and many were harder than their parents.
  quote: "approximately 8% of generated variants were effectively unsolvable (i.e. it took a symbolic system more than 5 seconds to solve)"
  where: p.4
- The verifier is numerical, not symbolic. It samples 5 random points in [-10, 10] and integrates over intervals of length 0.1. The tolerance is 1e-2 relative difference, with a 2-second timeout and up to 3 retries. The authors say the verifier "may not be 100% accurate".
  where: p.5
- The model exploited the verifier early on, and the authors added filters.
  quote: "models could exploit verification weaknesses by outputting trivial solutions (like the integration symbol itself) or degenerate forms"
  where: p.5
- The reward has two parts: an accuracy reward and a format reward for `<ANSWER>` tags. The KL coefficient is 0.001. The MIT run used batch size 128.
  where: p.6 and p.7
- Third-level variants were "trivially simple and lost mathematical relevance", so recursion was capped at depth 2 for the MIT run and depth 3 for Llama.
  where: p.7

LIMITS
- Only one domain is tested, integration, with a numerical checker.
- Test sets are tiny: 100 problems for Llama and 20 for the MIT exam. One question is 5 percentage points, and 73% of 20 is not a whole number of questions. The paper itself says "14/20" for 73%.
- TTRL uses the checker to decide "solved" at test time. The authors concede the o1 comparison is "a general baseline rather than a strict head-to-head evaluation" because o1 had no checker.
- The paper says harder-than-intended variants "consumed significant computational resources".
- Whether TTRL alone could work with enough compute is left open.
- The 90% is best-of-trajectory with oracle verification, not pass@1 from a single model.
- The "recursive decomposition" is generation of easier problems, not decomposition into subproblems of one solution.
- Claims about planning, agents, Lean and competitive programming are speculation (§5.2). The twin prime figure is illustrative only.
- Test-time compute cost and wall time are not reported. TTRL ran sequentially.
- The Llama 3B run reports no seeds or variance. Only the 7B run in Figure 5 is averaged over 3 runs.
- The paper has dated: it is a March 2025 preprint, with no peer-reviewed venue visible.
- Inconsistency: the introduction says "from 2% to 82%" where the abstract says 1%.

BUILDS ON
Haluptzok et al. 2023 (self-play programming puzzles checked by an interpreter); STaR (Zelikman et al. 2022); GRPO (Shao et al. 2024, DeepSeekMath); DeepSeek-R1 (2025); OpenAI o1 (2024); Chu et al. 2025 ("SFT memorizes, RL generalizes") and Logic-RL (Xie et al. 2025); Narvekar et al. 2020 (curriculum learning for RL); Let's Verify Step by Step (Lightman 2023); Tree of Thoughts (Yao 2023); self-consistency (Wang 2023); s1 (Muennighoff 2025). It does not cite Voyager.

CODE
Only pseudocode. Algorithm 1 (LADDER, p.4): generate N variants per training question, run GRPO on the variants, then sample test answers. Algorithm 2 (TTRL, p.4): per test question, generate variants, run GRPO from the base weights, answer, and roll back (§3.1.5). The GRPO advantage is Ai = (ri − mean) / std (Eq. 3, p.6).

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.3): the variant tree for an integral. It shows the root-to-leaf difficulty ladder and is the best single explainer of the method.
- Fig 2 (p.7): the LADDER training curve on Llama 3B, plateauing near 82% by about step 250-300.
- Fig 3 (p.7): test score against number of generated variants, up to 9k.
- Fig 4 (p.8): pass@1, pass@10, RL without variants and LADDER. It is the clearest ablation.
- Fig 5 (p.9): MIT Bee scores. Printed axis values are 32, 42, 50, 73 and 80. Labels are Claude-3.5, GPT-4o, base, LADDER and o1; I did not match each value to its bar, but the text supports 42 = GPT-4o, 50 = base, 73 = LADDER and 80 = o1.
- Fig 6 (p.10): LADDER pass@1 (73), pass@100, LADDER + TTRL (90) and the o1 line.
- Fig 7 (p.11): twin prime variant example (illustrative, weak).

FIT FOR NOTE 08
It fits the "weight-level self-improvement with verifiable rewards and an automatic curriculum" part of 08 well. Its relevance is the generate, solve, verify, learn cycle, with a model-built difficulty gradient and a programmatic verifier. It is not an agent-loop or Voyager-style skill library: it changes weights through GRPO, not prompts, memory or code. It fits partly in a verification or reward-hacking note (verifier exploits, p.5), and TTRL could be cited in a test-time-compute context. I would place it in 08 as a weights-level contrast to Voyager, with the caveat that the evidence comes from one narrow, small-n domain.

PROBLEMS
- Extraction of the formulas and the integrals in Figure 1 and the appendix is garbled, so I could not read the equations cleanly. The exact bar values in Figures 5 and 6 are unmatched to labels.
- No embedded instructions were found.
